investigations.title: Compare a changing gene pool
investigations.question: Can a change in allele frequency identify its cause without additional evidence?
investigations.sourceKind: synthetic genotype counts in a diploid model population

variables.compare: three observations of one model population
variables.observe: AA, Aa, aa and allele frequency
variables.holdConstant: locus, diploid counting rule and classification method

investigations.prediction: Predict what observation would support immigration rather than selective survival as the main explanation.
procedure: Compute N and the A-copy count 2AA+Aa at each observation, then divide by 2N.
Calculate expected genotype frequencies from each observed p and q under equilibrium assumptions; distinguish expectations from observations.
Compare the time series. Record what is missing about movement, births, deaths and sampling.
Propose one controlled simulation comparison and one field observation that could distinguish explanations; revise a claim that changing p proves selection.
investigations.expected: N=100 each time; p is 0.60,0.675,0.65 and q is 0.40,0.325,0.35. Initial expected frequencies are 0.36,0.48,0.16. Counts alone cannot distinguish movement, selection and sampling. The labelled movement observation is a model condition, not a conclusion proved by the genotype counts. Later equilibrium expected AA/Aa/aa frequencies are 0.455625/0.43875/0.105625 and 0.4225/0.455/0.1225; multiply each by 100 for expected counts. These expectations are conditional, not the observed counts.
limitations: Population counts are synthetic and no unique causal inference follows from frequency change alone.
Equilibrium genotype proportions at one time do not prove all assumptions.
investigations.collaborationEvidence: Independent planning, comparison and revision are observable here. Live teamwork and physical laboratory performance are not certified.

investigations.title: Separate within-species and between-species effects
investigations.question: How does the identity of nearby plants affect growth when total starting density is controlled?
investigations.sourceKind: synthetic plant microcosm data; units are dry mass per focal plant

variables.compare: neighbour identity and total initial density
variables.observe: mean dry mass per focal A plant after 30 days
variables.holdConstant: pot size, light, water, soil, measurement time

investigations.prediction: Predict which comparison estimates a density effect and which comparison changes neighbour identity at the same total density.
procedure: Identify focal A, the response unit, the comparison groups and one possible confounder.
Calculate replicate means. Compare 5 A with 10 A for a within-species density effect.
Compare 10 A with 5 A+5 B at the same total density; note that focal A density also differs, limiting isolation of a single mechanism.
Propose an additional density-series design and explain why reduced mass alone does not identify which resource was limiting.
investigations.expected: Means are 4.0,3.0,2.4 g per A plant. More A neighbours are associated with lower mean mass. Mixed pots have still lower focal A mass at the same total density, consistent with a neighbour-identity effect; resource measurements and more treatment combinations would be needed to establish a mechanism.
limitations: Two synthetic replicates illustrate comparison logic, not statistical significance.
The endpoint is plant mass rather than population growth rate.

investigations.title: Sample, estimate and explain change
investigations.question: How sensitive is a population estimate to the sampled area and its spatial pattern?
investigations.sourceKind: synthetic quadrat counts and independent whole-population demographic scenario

variables.observe: counts per quadrat and their spread
variables.holdConstant: species, quadrat area, observation date and counting method

investigations.prediction: Predict how choosing only visibly crowded quadrats would change the estimate.
procedure: Compute density as total individuals divided by total sampled area, then scale to the stated habitat area.
Compare the spread of counts and explain why an estimate from five quadrats needs uncertainty. Propose stratified sampling if habitat regions differ.
Use the separate demographic scenario to calculate ΔN, final N, growth rate and interval per-capita change. Label each denominator and unit.
Construct a two-point N-versus-time graph, then explain why two points do not distinguish exponential from logistic growth.
investigations.expected: Counts total 30 over 5 m², density 6 individuals/m², estimate 1200 across 200 m². Separate scenario: ΔN=120+30−70−20=60; final N=1060; growth rate=6 individuals/day; interval per-capita change=60/1000=0.06=6% over ten days. A time-normalized average is 0.006/day, a different quantity.
limitations: The quadrat estimate and demographic scenario are different model populations.
Sparse samples and two time points cannot establish carrying capacity or a curve shape.
investigations.collaborationEvidence: Independent planning, comparison and revision are observable here. Live teamwork and physical laboratory performance are not certified.
